title: Pairing Up to Launch the Second Wave

scenes.visual: Title card 'Pairing Up to Launch the Second Wave' fades over the same 2D cell cross-section and shared colour map from the first film (slate-blue membrane, dark cytosol, deep-indigo nucleus, white DNA bar; amber 'P', violet CREB, sky-blue NFAT, mint mRNA), adding gold-ochre Jun rods (#FBBF24) and magenta-pink Fos rods (#E879F9).

scenes.tts: In the first film, signals flipped pre-made factors to launch genes in minutes. How does a cell build many distinct DNA switches from few genes, and stretch a brief signal into hours?
scenes.caption: In the first film, signals flipped pre-made factors to launch genes in minutes. How does a cell build many distinct DNA switches from few genes, and stretch a brief signal into hours?
scenes.visual: Brief motion callback inside the carried cell cross-section: violet CREB gains an amber 'P' and sky-blue NFAT glides into the nucleus, sparking a brief flash of mint mRNA. A small schematic clock icon ticks from 'minutes' toward 'hours' as the opening question appears cleanly at top.
scenes.narration: In the first film, signals flipped pre-made factors to launch genes in minutes. How does a cell build many distinct DNA switches from few genes, and stretch a brief signal into hours?

scenes.tts: Many nuclear factors belong to the basic leucine zipper, or b-zip, family, including Creb. A b-zip protein cannot grip DNA well alone; it works as a pair. Two helices zip along a stripe of leucines. Below that zipper, positively charged tips, drawn to negatively charged DNA, part like chopsticks to grip two half-sites.
scenes.caption: Many nuclear factors belong to the basic leucine zipper, or bZIP, family, including CREB. A bZIP protein cannot grip DNA well alone; it works as a pair. Two helices zip along a stripe of leucines. Below that zipper, positively charged tips, drawn to negatively charged DNA, part like chopsticks to grip two half-sites.
scenes.visual: Zoom onto the white DNA bar inside the nucleus. Two straight rods (initially violet for CREB) slide together; glowing dots along their upper seam zip them side by side ('Leucine zipper'), while their lower ends part like chopsticks with bright '+' marks ('Basic tips') gripping two adjacent highlighted slots on the DNA bar.
scenes.narration: Many nuclear factors belong to the basic leucine zipper, or bZIP, family, including CREB. A bZIP protein cannot grip DNA well alone; it works as a pair. Two helices zip along a stripe of leucines. Below that zipper, positively charged tips, drawn to negatively charged DNA, part like chopsticks to grip two half-sites.

scenes.tts: Pairing multiplies choices, because swapping one partner changes which DNA site the pair prefers. With n proteins that all pair freely, the count is n times n plus one, divided by two. That counts same-partner pairs plus mixed pairs. Take three proteins. Three times four is twelve; divided by two gives six distinct pairs.
scenes.caption: Pairing multiplies choices, because swapping one partner changes which DNA site the pair prefers. With n proteins that all pair freely, the count is n × (n + 1) / 2. That counts same-partner pairs plus mixed pairs. Take 3 proteins: 3 × 4 = 12; 12 / 2 = 6 distinct pairs.
scenes.visual: Above the DNA bar, a clean pairing matrix opens beside the formula 'Pairs = n(n + 1) / 2'. As spoken, 'n = 3' highlights three labelled rods (A, B, C), then '3 × 4 = 12' and '12 / 2 = 6' appear step by step while the 3×3 upper-triangle cells light up: 3 same-partner pairs on the diagonal (A-A, B-B, C-C) and 3 mixed pairs (A-B, A-C, B-C).
scenes.narration: Pairing multiplies choices, because swapping one partner changes which DNA site the pair prefers. With n proteins that all pair freely, the count is n × (n + 1) / 2. That counts same-partner pairs plus mixed pairs. Take 3 proteins: 3 × 4 = 12; 12 / 2 = 6 distinct pairs.

scenes.tts: In real cells, not every pair is stable. Two b-zip families, Jun and Fos, build the factor A P one. Jun pairs with Jun or with Fos. Fos cannot pair stably with itself, because negatively charged residues beside its zipper repel each other.
scenes.caption: In real cells, not every pair is stable. Two bZIP families, Jun and Fos, build the factor AP-1. Jun pairs with Jun or with Fos. Fos cannot pair stably with itself, because negatively charged residues beside its zipper repel each other.
scenes.visual: Replace the generic rods with gold-ochre 'Jun' rods and magenta-pink 'Fos' rods. A gold Jun-Jun pair zips cleanly onto DNA, and a magenta-gold Fos-Jun pair ('AP-1') snaps on even more tightly. Two magenta Fos rods approach each other, flashing small '-' repulsion arcs along their seams, and bounce apart.
scenes.narration: In real cells, not every pair is stable. Two bZIP families, Jun and Fos, build the factor AP-1. Jun pairs with Jun or with Fos. Fos cannot pair stably with itself, because negatively charged residues beside its zipper repel each other.

scenes.tts: Try the partner rule yourself. Suppose a cell makes two Jun proteins and two Fos proteins. Pause and predict: with no Fos-Fos pairs allowed, how many distinct pairs can form?
scenes.caption: Try the partner rule yourself. Suppose a cell makes 2 Jun proteins and 2 Fos proteins. Pause and predict: with no Fos–Fos pairs allowed, how many distinct pairs can form?
scenes.visual: A clean 4-by-4 upper-triangle pairing grid appears labelled 'J1, J2' (gold) and 'F1, F2' (magenta). The three Fos-Fos cells (F1-F1, F1-F2, F2-F2) are softly dimmed and marked 'x'. Prompt card above reads: '2 Jun + 2 Fos (no Fos–Fos) -> How many pairs?'.
scenes.narration: Try the partner rule yourself. Suppose a cell makes 2 Jun proteins and 2 Fos proteins. Pause and predict: with no Fos–Fos pairs allowed, how many distinct pairs can form?

scenes.visual: Thinking pause: keep the 2 Jun + 2 Fos grid and the prompt card on screen with a thin glowing progress bar sweeping smoothly across the bottom while the open Jun-Jun and Fos-Jun cells pulse gently.

scenes.tts: Seven pairs, because the rule removes only the Fos pairs. Two Jun proteins make three Jun pairs: two times three, divided by two, is three. Two Fos times two Jun add four mixed pairs. Three plus four is seven. Four free proteins would make four times five, over two, or ten.
scenes.caption: Seven pairs, because the rule removes only the Fos–Fos pairs. 2 Jun proteins make 3 Jun–Jun pairs: 2 × 3 / 2 = 3. 2 Fos × 2 Jun add 4 mixed pairs. 3 + 4 = 7. Four free proteins would make 4 × 5 / 2 = 10.
scenes.visual: Numbers appear in sync with speech: a bold '7 pairs' badge first, then the 3 gold Jun-Jun cells illuminate ('2 × 3 / 2 = 3'), then the 4 gold-magenta Fos-Jun cells illuminate ('2 × 2 = 4'), the dimmed Fos-Fos corner shows '+ 0', '3 + 4 = 7' appears, and finally a small comparison line '4 × 5 / 2 = 10 if free'.
scenes.narration: Seven pairs, because the rule removes only the Fos–Fos pairs. 2 Jun proteins make 3 Jun–Jun pairs: 2 × 3 / 2 = 3. 2 Fos × 2 Jun add 4 mixed pairs. 3 + 4 = 7. Four free proteins would make 4 × 5 / 2 = 10.

scenes.tts: Swapping partners also tunes DNA grip. A Fos-Jun pair holds DNA more tightly than Jun-Jun. It also prefers a seven-letter DNA site, one letter shorter than Creb's eight-letter site. Back to the first film's gene, C fos. Pre-made factors switch on C fos transcripts within minutes.
scenes.caption: Swapping partners also tunes DNA grip. A Fos–Jun pair holds DNA more tightly than Jun–Jun. It also prefers a 7-letter DNA site, one letter shorter than CREB's 8-letter site. Back to the first film's gene, c-fos. Pre-made factors switch on c-fos transcripts within minutes.
scenes.visual: Side-by-side on the white DNA bar, violet CREB sits over an 8-slot bar ('8 letters') while magenta-gold Fos-Jun grips a 7-slot bar ('7 letters') with a brighter glow than a dimmer gold Jun-Jun pair. Camera then pulls back to the carried cell cross-section as violet CREB launches mint 'c-fos mRNA' ribbons.
scenes.narration: Swapping partners also tunes DNA grip. A Fos–Jun pair holds DNA more tightly than Jun–Jun. It also prefers a 7-letter DNA site, one letter shorter than CREB's 8-letter site. Back to the first film's gene, c-fos. Pre-made factors switch on c-fos transcripts within minutes.

scenes.tts: When ribosomes are running, those transcripts build new Fos protein. Fos enters the nucleus and zips with Jun to form A P one. On immune genes like interleukin two, A P one sits beside N F A T from the first film. Two pathways then meet at one DNA site.
scenes.caption: When ribosomes are running, those transcripts build new Fos protein. Fos enters the nucleus and zips with Jun to form AP-1. On immune genes like interleukin-2, AP-1 sits beside NFAT from the first film. Two pathways then meet at one DNA site.
scenes.visual: In the cytosol, active ribosomes translate mint 'c-fos mRNA' into magenta 'Fos' rods. Fos glides through a nuclear pore, zips with gold 'Jun' onto the DNA bar as 'AP-1', and sky-blue 'NFAT' docks right beside AP-1 on a composite slot labelled 'IL-2 site'.
scenes.narration: When ribosomes are running, those transcripts build new Fos protein. Fos enters the nucleus and zips with Jun to form AP-1. On immune genes like interleukin-2, AP-1 sits beside NFAT from the first film. Two pathways then meet at one DNA site.

scenes.tts: Paired factors widen gene choices and drive a slower second wave. Newly assembled A P one switches on later genes over hours. Because that wave waits for newly made Fos and other first-wave proteins, a brief signal becomes a lasting program. Staining Fos hours later marks neurons that were strongly excited.
scenes.caption: Paired factors widen gene choices and drive a slower second wave. Newly assembled AP-1 switches on later genes over hours. Because that wave waits for newly made Fos and other first-wave proteins, a brief signal becomes a lasting program. Staining Fos hours later marks neurons that were strongly excited.
scenes.visual: A clean timeline graph labelled 'schematic' sweeps across the bottom of the cell view: a tall, quick mint peak ('First wave: c-fos, minutes') followed by a broader magenta-gold rise ('Second wave: AP-1 targets, hours'). In an upper inset, a row of schematic neurons in which only some have magenta-stained nuclei ('Fos stain, hours later').
scenes.narration: Paired factors widen gene choices and drive a slower second wave. Newly assembled AP-1 switches on later genes over hours. Because that wave waits for newly made Fos and other first-wave proteins, a brief signal becomes a lasting program. Staining Fos hours later marks neurons that were strongly excited.
